questions.q: The fusion of the nuclei of a sperm and an egg is called
questions.explain: Fertilisation is the fusion of the nucleus of a sperm with the nucleus of an egg. It forms a fertilised egg.
questions.lo: Recognise that the union of the nuclei of an egg and a sperm (inputs) forms a fertilised egg that develops into a new individual (output)

notes.0: Ovulation is the release of an egg from an ovary. It happens before the egg can meet a sperm.
notes.1: Ejaculation is the release of semen from the penis. It delivers sperm but does not join the sperm and egg nuclei.
notes.2: Menstruation is the breakdown and discharge of the uterine lining. It does not involve a sperm at all.

questions.q: When an egg cell is fertilised, it develops into
questions.explain: A fertilised egg divides many times to form an embryo, which grows into a new individual.
questions.lo: Recognise that the union of the nuclei of an egg and a sperm (inputs) forms a fertilised egg that develops into a new individual (output)

notes.0: Sperm cells are made in the testes of a male. A fertilised egg does not turn back into a sex cell.
notes.2: Semen is the fluid of sperm and nutrient fluid made by the male. It does not come from a fertilised egg.
notes.3: The ovary is the organ that produces eggs. A fertilised egg develops into a new individual, not into an organ of the mother.

why.right: A fertilised egg becomes an embryo because it divides many times to form a ball of cells.
wrong: A fertilised egg becomes an embryo because it joins with more sperm to grow larger.
A fertilised egg becomes an embryo because it takes in cells from the wall of the ovary.

questions.q: In sexual reproduction as a system, what are the inputs?
questions.explain: The inputs are what go into the process. An egg and a sperm go in, and their nuclei fuse to form a fertilised egg.
questions.lo: Recognise that the union of the nuclei of an egg and a sperm (inputs) forms a fertilised egg that develops into a new individual (output)

notes.1: An embryo and a foetus are stages that develop after fertilisation. They come out of the process, not into it.
notes.2: A fertilised egg is formed when the nuclei fuse. It is produced by the process, so it is not an input.
notes.3: A new individual is the final result of the process. That makes it the output, not the input.

why.right: The egg and sperm are the inputs because they go into the process before their nuclei fuse.
wrong: The egg and sperm are the inputs because they are produced at the very end of the process.
The egg and sperm are the inputs because they grow into a foetus without their nuclei fusing.

questions.q: The passing down of genetic material from one generation to the next is
questions.explain: Heredity is the passing of genetic material from parents to offspring, from one generation to the next.
questions.lo: Recognise that sexual reproduction passes genetic material from one generation to the next (heredity)

notes.0: Ovulation is the release of an egg from an ovary. It is one event in a woman's cycle, not the passing on of genetic material.
notes.1: Fertilisation is the fusion of a sperm nucleus and an egg nucleus. It is one event, not the passing of traits across generations.
notes.3: Puberty is the stage when the body becomes able to reproduce. It is not the passing on of genetic material.

questions.q: Which disease can be passed from parent to child in the genetic material?
questions.explain: Sickle cell anaemia is caused by genetic material. It can be passed from parents to a child through the egg and sperm.
questions.lo: Recognise that sexual reproduction passes genetic material from one generation to the next (heredity)

notes.0: Influenza is caused by a virus that spreads from person to person through the air. It is not carried in genetic material.
notes.2: Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria that spread through the air. It is not carried in genetic material.
notes.3: Typhoid is caused by bacteria in dirty food or water. It is not carried in genetic material.

why.right: Sickle cell anaemia is inherited because it is caused by genetic material passed on in the egg or sperm.
wrong: Sickle cell anaemia is inherited because it is caused by germs passed on in the mother's milk.
Sickle cell anaemia is inherited because it is caused by bacteria passed on in the air at home.

questions.q: Genetic material from the mother is passed to the child in the
questions.explain: The egg comes from the mother. The genetic material in the nucleus of the egg is passed to the child at fertilisation.
questions.lo: Explain similarities and differences between offspring, parents and siblings using the unique combination of genetic material from egg and sperm

notes.0: The uterine lining nourishes the developing embryo. It does not pass genetic material to the child.
notes.1: Nutrient fluid is made by the male sex glands to nourish sperm. It does not carry the mother's genetic material.
notes.2: The sperm comes from the father. Its nucleus carries the father's genetic material, not the mother's.

why.right: The child gets the mother's genetic material because the egg nucleus, made by the mother, fuses with the sperm nucleus.
wrong: The child gets the mother's genetic material because the uterine lining passes it to the embryo during pregnancy.
The child gets the mother's genetic material because the sperm collects it from the mother's body before fertilisation.

questions.q: A girl has her father's nose and her mother's eye colour. This shows she
choices: inherited traits from her father only
inherited traits from her mother only
questions.explain: The girl has a trait from her father and a trait from her mother. This shows she inherited genetic material from both parents.
questions.lo: Explain similarities and differences between offspring, parents and siblings using the unique combination of genetic material from egg and sperm

notes.1: Being identical would mean every trait is the same. She has a mix of traits, so she is not identical to either parent.
notes.2: Her eye colour comes from her mother. Look at where each of her traits came from.
notes.3: Her nose comes from her father. Look at where each of her traits came from.

why.right: She has traits of both parents because she received genetic material from both the egg and the sperm.
wrong: She has traits of both parents because she copies the features of the parent she sees most.
She has traits of both parents because the uterus shapes her features to match her family.

questions.q: Two sisters have the same parents but look different. Why?
choices: only one has the father's genetic material
genetic material is not passed to daughters
each has a unique mix of genetic material
only one has the mother's genetic material
questions.explain: Each egg and each sperm carries a different mix of genetic material. Each sister formed from a different egg and sperm, so each has a unique mix.
questions.lo: Explain similarities and differences between offspring, parents and siblings using the unique combination of genetic material from egg and sperm

notes.0: Both sisters received genetic material from the father through a sperm. The difference is in which mix each one received.
notes.1: Genetic material is passed to every child, sons and daughters alike. Both sisters inherited it from their parents.
notes.3: Both sisters received genetic material from the mother through an egg. The difference is in which mix each one received.

why.right: Sisters look different because each formed from a different egg and sperm with a different mix of genetic material.
wrong: Sisters look different because the older one takes more genetic material from the parents than the younger one.
Sisters look different because their genetic material keeps changing as each child grows up after birth.

questions.q: Puberty begins when the body produces certain
questions.explain: Puberty begins when the body starts to produce sex hormones. These hormones cause the physical changes of puberty.
questions.lo: State the physical changes in males and females during puberty caused by hormones

notes.0: Vaccines are given to protect against diseases. The body does not make them, and they do not start puberty.
notes.1: Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria. They do not start the body changes of puberty.
notes.3: Nutrient fluids are made by the sex glands to nourish sperm. They are not chemical messengers that start body changes.

questions.q: During puberty, the voice deepens. This change happens in
questions.explain: A deeper voice is a change that male sex hormones cause in males during puberty.
questions.lo: State the physical changes in males and females during puberty caused by hormones

notes.1: Female sex hormones do not make the voice deepen. This change is caused by the hormones of the other sex.
notes.2: Some changes happen in both sexes, but a deeper voice is caused by the hormones of only one sex.

questions.q: During puberty, the hips become broader and rounder. This change happens in
questions.explain: Broader, rounder hips are a change caused by female sex hormones in females during puberty.
questions.lo: State the physical changes in males and females during puberty caused by hormones

notes.0: Some changes happen in both sexes, but broader hips are caused by the hormones of only one sex.
notes.2: Male sex hormones make the shoulders broader, not the hips. Broader hips are caused by the hormones of the other sex.

questions.q: During puberty, pubic hair appears. This change happens in
questions.explain: Pubic hair grows in both males and females during puberty.
questions.lo: State the physical changes in males and females during puberty caused by hormones

notes.0: Pubic hair does not grow in females only. Think about the changes that take place in the other sex as well.
notes.2: Pubic hair does not grow in males only. Think about the changes that take place in the other sex as well.

questions.q: Which part of the male reproductive system produces sperm?
questions.explain: The testes produce sperm. They also produce male sex hormones.
questions.lo: State the functions of the parts of the male reproductive system

notes.0: The sperm duct carries sperm from where they are made to the urethra. It does not make them.
notes.1: The urethra carries semen or urine out of the body. It does not make sperm.
notes.2: The sex glands produce nutrient fluid that nourishes sperm. They do not make the sperm.

questions.q: What is the function of the sperm duct?
choices: carries sperm from the testes to the urethra
questions.explain: The sperm duct is a tube that carries sperm from the testes to the urethra.
questions.lo: State the functions of the parts of the male reproductive system

notes.0: Nutrient fluid is made by the sex glands. The sperm duct is a tube that moves sperm.
notes.1: The penis deposits semen into the vagina. The sperm duct is a tube inside the body.
notes.2: Sperm are produced in the testes. The sperm duct carries them but does not make them.

questions.q: What is the function of the sex glands?
choices: produce nutrient fluid to nourish sperm
questions.explain: The sex glands produce nutrient fluid that nourishes the sperm.
questions.lo: State the functions of the parts of the male reproductive system

notes.1: Carrying sperm to the urethra is the job of the sperm duct. The sex glands add a fluid to the sperm.
notes.2: Sperm are produced in the testes. The sex glands add a fluid to the sperm.
notes.3: Urine is made by the kidneys and leaves through the urethra. The sex glands are part of the reproductive system.

questions.q: Semen is made up of
questions.explain: Semen is made of sperm from the testes mixed with nutrient fluid from the sex glands.
questions.lo: State the functions of the parts of the male reproductive system

notes.0: Urine and semen both leave through the urethra, but never at the same time. Urine is not part of semen.
notes.1: Semen carries the male sex cells. A fluid with no sex cells in it would not be semen.
notes.3: Eggs are produced by females in the ovaries. Semen is made only by the male reproductive system.

questions.q: Which male part carries both semen and urine?
questions.explain: The urethra is the tube through the penis. It carries semen during ejaculation and urine at other times.
questions.lo: State the functions of the parts of the male reproductive system

notes.0: The sperm duct carries sperm only. It joins the tube that also carries urine.
notes.1: The testis produces sperm and male sex hormones. It does not carry urine.
notes.3: The sex glands produce nutrient fluid. They do not carry urine.

why.right: The urethra carries both because the tube from the bladder and the sperm ducts both join it.
wrong: The urethra carries both because semen and urine are mixed together in the bladder first.
The urethra carries both because the testes make urine as well as sperm.

questions.q: Which male part deposits semen into the vagina?
questions.explain: The penis deposits semen into the vagina during sexual intercourse.
questions.lo: State the functions of the parts of the male reproductive system

notes.0: The sex glands make nutrient fluid inside the body. They do not deposit semen.
notes.2: The sperm duct carries sperm inside the body to the urethra. It does not deposit semen into the vagina.
notes.3: The testis produces sperm inside the body. It does not deposit semen.

questions.q: Besides sperm, the testes also produce
questions.explain: The testes produce sperm and male sex hormones. These hormones cause the male changes during puberty.
questions.lo: State the functions of the parts of the male reproductive system

notes.1: Nutrient fluid is made by the sex glands. The testes make something that causes the changes of puberty.
notes.2: Eggs are produced by the ovaries in females. The testes are male organs.
notes.3: Urine is made by the kidneys. The testes are part of the reproductive system.

questions.q: Which part of the female reproductive system produces eggs?
questions.explain: The ovaries produce eggs. They also produce female sex hormones.
questions.lo: State the functions of the parts of the female reproductive system

notes.0: The cervix is the opening of the uterus. It does not make eggs.
notes.1: The oviduct carries the egg after it is released. It does not make the egg.
notes.2: The uterus is where the embryo develops. It does not make eggs.

questions.q: Where does fertilisation usually take place?
questions.explain: Fertilisation usually takes place in the oviduct, where the released egg meets the sperm.
questions.lo: State the functions of the parts of the female reproductive system

notes.0: The uterus is where the embryo implants and develops. The egg and sperm usually meet before the egg gets there.
notes.1: The ovary releases the egg, but sperm do not reach the ovary. The egg meets the sperm after it leaves the ovary.
notes.3: Sperm are deposited in the vagina but must swim much further to meet the egg.

why.right: Fertilisation happens in the oviduct because the released egg travels along it and sperm swim up to meet it.
wrong: Fertilisation happens in the oviduct because the oviduct produces eggs and stores sperm until they meet.
Fertilisation happens in the oviduct because the embryo must implant in the oviduct wall straight after.

questions.q: In which organ does an embryo develop into a foetus?
questions.explain: The embryo implants in the wall of the uterus and develops into a foetus there.
questions.lo: State the functions of the parts of the female reproductive system

notes.0: The vagina is the birth canal. The baby passes through it at birth, but it does not develop there.
notes.1: The oviduct is where fertilisation usually happens. The embryo moves on from there to develop.
notes.2: The ovary produces eggs. The embryo does not develop in the ovary.

why.right: The embryo develops in the uterus because the thick uterine lining supports it and supplies food and oxygen.
wrong: The embryo develops in the uterus because the uterus produces the eggs that become the foetus.
The embryo develops in the uterus because the uterus is the narrow tube where sperm meet the egg.

questions.q: What is the cervix?
questions.explain: The cervix is the narrow opening of the uterus. It leads into the vagina.
questions.lo: State the functions of the parts of the female reproductive system

notes.0: The tube from the ovary is the oviduct. The cervix is at the other end of the uterus.
notes.2: The organ that produces eggs is the ovary. The cervix does not make eggs.
notes.3: The lining of the uterus is the layer inside it that thickens each month. The cervix is a different part.

questions.q: Which part is also known as the birth canal?
questions.explain: The vagina is called the birth canal because the baby passes through it during birth.
questions.lo: State the functions of the parts of the female reproductive system

notes.1: The oviduct carries the egg from the ovary to the uterus. The baby does not pass through it.
notes.2: The cervix is the opening of the uterus. The baby passes through it, but it is not the canal itself.
notes.3: The uterus is where the baby develops. The birth canal is the passage the baby travels along to leave the body.

questions.q: Which part is NOT part of the female reproductive system?
questions.explain: In females the urethra carries urine only. It belongs to the excretory system, not the reproductive system.
questions.lo: State the functions of the parts of the female reproductive system

notes.0: The vagina receives sperm and is the birth canal. It is part of the female reproductive system.
notes.2: The cervix is the opening of the uterus. It is part of the female reproductive system.
notes.3: The oviduct carries the egg and is where fertilisation happens. It is part of the female reproductive system.

questions.q: Which is the correct path of sperm in the male body?
questions.explain: Sperm are made in the testis, travel along the sperm duct and leave the body through the urethra.
questions.lo: Trace the path of sperm and egg in fertilisation and the development that follows

notes.0: The urethra is where sperm leave the body, so it comes last. Think about where sperm are made.
notes.1: The sperm duct connects the testis to the urethra. Sperm must pass along it before they reach the urethra.
notes.3: Sperm are made before they travel. The organ that makes them must come first.

why.right: Sperm follow this path because they are made in the testis and carried by the sperm duct to the urethra.
wrong: Sperm follow this path because they are made in the sex glands and then stored in the testis.
Sperm follow this path because urine pushes them out of the testis and into the urethra.

questions.q: Which is the correct path of sperm in the female body?
questions.explain: Sperm are deposited in the vagina, pass through the cervix into the uterus, then swim into the oviduct to meet the egg.
questions.lo: Trace the path of sperm and egg in fertilisation and the development that follows

notes.0: The cervix opens into the uterus. Sperm must pass through the uterus before they reach the oviduct.
notes.1: Sperm are deposited in the vagina, so the vagina comes first. Think about where the penis places the semen.
notes.2: The cervix is between the vagina and the uterus. Sperm pass through it before they enter the uterus.

why.right: Sperm follow this path because they swim from the vagina through the cervix and uterus to reach the egg.
wrong: Sperm follow this path because the uterus pumps them into the oviduct to make new eggs.
Sperm follow this path because the egg is made in the uterus and then moves to the oviduct.

questions.q: Which order of development after fertilisation is correct?
questions.explain: The fertilised egg divides to form an embryo. The embryo grows into a foetus, which develops into a baby.
questions.lo: Trace the path of sperm and egg in fertilisation and the development that follows

notes.1: This order runs backwards. Development starts from the cell formed when the nuclei fuse.
notes.2: The embryo is the early stage that forms first. A foetus is a later stage with recognisable body parts.
notes.3: An embryo forms when the fertilised egg divides. It cannot come before the fertilised egg.

why.right: Development follows this order because the fertilised egg divides to form an embryo that grows into a foetus.
wrong: Development follows this order because the embryo is fertilised a second time to become a foetus.
Development follows this order because the fertilised egg must leave the uterus to become an embryo.

questions.q: Where is the embryo implanted?
questions.explain: The embryo implants in the thick wall of the uterus, which supplies it with food and oxygen.
questions.lo: Trace the path of sperm and egg in fertilisation and the development that follows

notes.1: Fertilisation happens in the oviduct, but the embryo moves on. It implants where the lining has thickened for it.
notes.2: The ovary produces eggs. The embryo does not return to the ovary.
notes.3: The cervix is the narrow opening of the uterus. The embryo implants in a thicker, softer part.

why.right: The embryo implants in the uterus wall because its thick lining can supply the embryo with food and oxygen.
wrong: The embryo implants in the uterus wall because this is where the sperm first meets the egg.
The embryo implants in the uterus wall because the uterus produces new eggs to feed the embryo.

questions.q: After one sperm nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus, the other sperm
choices: fuse with the egg as well
questions.explain: Only one sperm nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus. The other sperm do not fuse and soon die.
questions.lo: Trace the path of sperm and egg in fertilisation and the development that follows

notes.0: Only one sperm nucleus can fuse with the egg nucleus. After that, no other sperm can join.
notes.1: An embryo forms from a fertilised egg. A sperm on its own cannot develop into an embryo.
notes.2: Sperm cannot swim back to where they were made. They stay in the female body.

questions.q: A man's testes cannot produce healthy sperm. What is the effect?
questions.explain: Without healthy sperm, no sperm nucleus can fuse with the egg nucleus. Fertilisation cannot occur.
questions.lo: Predict how a disrupted part of a reproductive system affects fertilisation

notes.0: Ovulation is controlled by the woman's own body. The man's sperm do not affect the release of her eggs.
notes.1: The uterine lining thickens during the woman's monthly cycle. This does not depend on the man's sperm.
notes.3: Urine leaves through the urethra. The testes do not make urine, so this is not affected.

why.right: Fertilisation cannot occur because there is no healthy sperm nucleus to fuse with the egg nucleus.
wrong: Fertilisation cannot occur because the woman needs sperm before her ovaries can release an egg.
Fertilisation cannot occur because the testes also make the eggs that the sperm fuse with.

questions.q: A woman's oviducts are blocked. Why can fertilisation not occur?
questions.explain: The oviduct is where sperm meet the egg. If it is blocked, sperm cannot reach the egg, so fertilisation cannot occur.
questions.lo: Predict how a disrupted part of a reproductive system affects fertilisation

notes.0: Eggs are produced in the ovaries, which still work. The problem is in the tube the egg travels along.
notes.2: The uterine lining is not in the oviducts. The blockage is in the tube where the egg and sperm meet.
notes.3: Sperm are still deposited in the vagina. The problem is further along the path the sperm travel.

why.right: Blocked oviducts stop fertilisation because sperm cannot travel along them to meet the egg.
wrong: Blocked oviducts stop fertilisation because the oviducts are where the eggs are made.
Blocked oviducts stop fertilisation because the uterine lining grows inside the oviducts.

questions.q: The release of an egg from an ovary is called
questions.explain: Ovulation is the release of an egg from an ovary. In a 28-day cycle it happens around day 14.
questions.lo: Describe the phases of the 28-day menstrual cycle and identify the phase on a given day

notes.0: Fertilisation is the fusion of a sperm nucleus and an egg nucleus. It can only happen after the egg is released.
notes.2: Menstruation is the breakdown and discharge of the uterine lining. It does not involve releasing an egg.
notes.3: Implantation is when an embryo sinks into the uterine wall. It happens after fertilisation, not when an egg leaves the ovary.

questions.q: Menstruation is the
choices: release of an egg from an ovary
breakdown and discharge of the uterine lining
fusion of a sperm and an egg
questions.explain: Menstruation is the breakdown and discharge of the uterine lining. In a 28-day cycle it happens on days 1 to 5.
questions.lo: Describe the phases of the 28-day menstrual cycle and identify the phase on a given day

notes.0: The release of an egg from an ovary is ovulation, a different event in the cycle.
notes.1: Thickening of the lining is the repair that follows. Menstruation is when the lining is lost.
notes.3: The fusion of a sperm and an egg is fertilisation. Menstruation happens when no fertilisation has taken place.

questions.q: Why does the uterine lining thicken?
choices: to prepare for implantation of an embryo
questions.explain: The uterine lining thickens to prepare for an embryo to implant. A thick lining can supply the embryo with food and oxygen.
questions.lo: Describe the phases of the 28-day menstrual cycle and identify the phase on a given day

notes.1: Sperm are nourished by the nutrient fluid from the male sex glands. The lining prepares for something that forms after fertilisation.
notes.2: The uterine lining does not kill sperm. It thickens to support something that forms after fertilisation.
notes.3: Eggs are produced in the ovaries. The uterine lining does not make eggs.

why.right: The uterine lining thickens because an embryo needs a thick lining to implant in and be supplied with food.
wrong: The uterine lining thickens because an egg needs a thick lining to be produced in each month.
The uterine lining thickens because sperm need a thick lining to swim through to reach the egg.

questions.q: A woman has a 28-day cycle. What happens on days 1 to 5?
questions.explain: Days 1 to 5 of a 28-day cycle are menstruation, when the uterine lining breaks down and is discharged.
questions.lo: Describe the phases of the 28-day menstrual cycle and identify the phase on a given day

notes.0: The fertile period is around the middle of the cycle, about days 10 to 17. Days 1 to 5 are at the start.
notes.1: Repair of the lining comes after it has broken down, around days 6 to 9. Days 1 to 5 come before that.
notes.2: Ovulation happens around day 14, in the middle of the cycle. Days 1 to 5 are at the start.

questions.q: A woman has a 28-day cycle. What happens on days 6 to 9?
questions.explain: Days 6 to 9 are the repair phase. The uterine lining starts to thicken again after menstruation.
questions.lo: Describe the phases of the 28-day menstrual cycle and identify the phase on a given day

notes.0: The lining breaks down at the start of the cycle, on days 1 to 5. By days 6 to 9 that phase has ended.
notes.1: Menstruation takes place on days 1 to 5. By days 6 to 9 that phase has ended.
notes.2: Ovulation happens around day 14. Days 6 to 9 come before it.

questions.q: A woman has a 28-day cycle. On about which day is ovulation?
questions.explain: In a 28-day cycle, ovulation happens around day 14, in the middle of the cycle.
questions.lo: Describe the phases of the 28-day menstrual cycle and identify the phase on a given day

notes.0: Day 28 is the last day of the cycle, just before the next menstruation. Ovulation happens much earlier.
notes.2: Day 1 is the first day of menstruation. Ovulation happens later in the cycle.
notes.3: Day 5 is the end of menstruation. Ovulation happens later in the cycle.

questions.q: A woman has a 28-day cycle. On day 12, she is in the
choices: repair phase of the uterine lining
questions.explain: The fertile period in a 28-day cycle is about days 10 to 17. Day 12 falls within it.
questions.lo: Describe the phases of the 28-day menstrual cycle and identify the phase on a given day

notes.0: The repair phase is days 6 to 9. Day 12 comes after it.
notes.1: Menstruation is days 1 to 5. Day 12 is well after it.

why.right: Day 12 is in the fertile period because it falls between about day 10 and day 17.
wrong: Day 12 is in the fertile period because ovulation happens on day 12 in every cycle.
Day 12 is in the fertile period because the uterine lining breaks down on that day.

questions.q: Menstruation began on 1 June. In a 28-day cycle, ovulation is expected around
questions.explain: 1 June is day 1 of the cycle. Ovulation happens around day 14, which is 14 June.
questions.lo: Describe the phases of the 28-day menstrual cycle and identify the phase on a given day

notes.1: 5 June is day 5, the end of menstruation. Ovulation happens in the middle of the cycle.
notes.2: 1 June is day 1, the start of menstruation. Ovulation happens later in the cycle.
notes.3: 28 June is day 28, the end of the cycle. Ovulation happens in the middle of the cycle.

why.right: Ovulation is expected on 14 June because 1 June is day 1 and ovulation is around day 14.
wrong: Ovulation is expected on 14 June because ovulation happens 14 days after menstruation ends.
Ovulation is expected on 14 June because ovulation happens halfway through each calendar month.

questions.q: Why does the fertile period begin a few days before ovulation?
choices: an egg survives for about a month
sperm are produced in the ovary
the uterine lining is breaking down
sperm can survive for three to five days
questions.explain: Sperm can survive in the female body for three to five days. Sperm deposited a few days before ovulation can still fertilise the egg.
questions.lo: Describe the phases of the 28-day menstrual cycle and identify the phase on a given day

notes.0: An egg survives for only about a day after it is released, not a month.
notes.1: Sperm are produced in the testes of a male. The ovary produces eggs.
notes.2: The lining breaks down during menstruation, at the start of the cycle. This does not explain the timing of the fertile period.

why.right: The fertile period starts early because sperm can live for several days while waiting for an egg to be released.
wrong: The fertile period starts early because the egg is released several days before ovulation takes place.
The fertile period starts early because sperm take several days to swim from the vagina to the ovary.

questions.q: A dome-shaped plastic cover is placed over the cervix. Which method is this?
questions.explain: A diaphragm is a dome-shaped cover placed over the cervix. It stops sperm from entering the uterus.
questions.lo: Identify how temporary and permanent birth control methods prevent conception

notes.1: An intra-uterine device is placed inside the uterus, not over the cervix.
notes.2: Spermicide is a chemical that kills sperm. It is not a plastic cover.
notes.3: A condom is worn over the penis. It is not placed over the cervix.

questions.q: The oviducts are cut and tied. Which method is this?
questions.explain: Tubal ligation is the cutting and tying of the oviducts. Eggs can no longer meet sperm.
questions.lo: Identify how temporary and permanent birth control methods prevent conception

notes.0: A vasectomy cuts and ties the sperm ducts in a male. The oviducts are in a female.
notes.1: A diaphragm is a dome-shaped cover over the cervix. It does not involve cutting any tubes.
notes.3: An intra-uterine device is placed inside the uterus. It does not involve cutting any tubes.

questions.q: The sperm ducts are cut and tied. Which method is this?
questions.explain: A vasectomy is the cutting and tying of the sperm ducts. Sperm can no longer reach the urethra.
questions.lo: Identify how temporary and permanent birth control methods prevent conception

notes.0: Tubal ligation cuts and ties the oviducts in a female. The sperm ducts are in a male.
notes.2: A condom is a cover worn over the penis. It does not involve cutting any tubes.
notes.3: Spermicide is a chemical that kills sperm. It does not involve cutting any tubes.

questions.q: A couple avoids sexual intercourse during the fertile period. Which method is this?
questions.explain: The rhythm method avoids sexual intercourse during the fertile period, when an egg may be present to be fertilised.
questions.lo: Identify how temporary and permanent birth control methods prevent conception

notes.1: Birth control pills contain hormones that disrupt the release of eggs. They do not depend on timing.
notes.2: A condom stops sperm from entering the vagina. It does not depend on timing.
notes.3: Spermicide is a chemical that kills sperm. It does not depend on timing.

why.right: The rhythm method works because sperm are kept away during the days when an egg may be fertilised.
wrong: The rhythm method works because no eggs are released at all during the fertile period.
The rhythm method works because sperm cannot survive in the body during the fertile period.

questions.q: How do birth control pills prevent pregnancy?
choices: they disrupt the release of eggs
they kill sperm in the vagina
questions.explain: Birth control pills contain hormones that disrupt the release of eggs. With no egg released, fertilisation cannot occur.
questions.lo: Identify how temporary and permanent birth control methods prevent conception

notes.0: Cutting the oviducts is tubal ligation, a surgery. Pills are taken by mouth and act through hormones.
notes.2: A cover over the cervix is a diaphragm. Pills are taken by mouth and act through hormones.
notes.3: Killing sperm is what spermicide does. Pills act on the woman's own body through hormones.

why.right: Birth control pills work because their hormones stop the ovaries from releasing eggs.
wrong: Birth control pills work because their chemicals kill the sperm inside the uterus.
Birth control pills work because their hormones stop the testes from making sperm.

questions.q: Besides blocking fertilisation, an intra-uterine device also prevents
questions.explain: An intra-uterine device in the uterus makes it hard for an embryo to implant in the uterine wall.
questions.lo: Identify how temporary and permanent birth control methods prevent conception

notes.0: Sperm are produced in the testes of the male. A device in the woman's uterus does not affect their production.
notes.1: Menstruation still happens with an intra-uterine device in place. Think about what happens in the uterus after fertilisation.
notes.2: Eggs are released from the ovaries. A device inside the uterus does not stop the ovaries from working.

why.right: An intra-uterine device stops pregnancy because it makes it hard for an embryo to implant in the uterus wall.
wrong: An intra-uterine device stops pregnancy because it releases hormones that stop sperm from being made.
An intra-uterine device stops pregnancy because it removes the uterine lining every day.

questions.q: A couple has decided to have no more children. Which method suits them?
questions.explain: Tubal ligation is a permanent method. It suits a couple who have decided to have no more children.
questions.lo: Identify how temporary and permanent birth control methods prevent conception

notes.0: Spermicide is a temporary method that must be used each time. The couple want a method that lasts for good.
notes.1: A condom is a temporary method that must be used each time. The couple want a method that lasts for good.
notes.3: The rhythm method is temporary and not very reliable. The couple want a method that lasts for good.

why.right: Tubal ligation suits them because it is a permanent method that stops eggs from meeting sperm.
wrong: Tubal ligation suits them because it is a temporary method that can be stopped at any time.
Tubal ligation suits them because it stops the man's testes from making any more sperm.

questions.q: After a vasectomy, the semen released during ejaculation
questions.explain: A vasectomy cuts and ties the sperm ducts. Semen is still released, but it contains no sperm.
questions.lo: Identify how temporary and permanent birth control methods prevent conception

notes.0: Semen can still leave the body through the urethra. Only the sperm ducts are cut.
notes.1: Cutting the sperm ducts stops sperm from reaching the urethra. The amount of sperm does not go up.
notes.3: Nutrient fluid comes from the sex glands, which are not cut. The cut tubes carry something else.

why.right: The semen has no sperm because the cut sperm ducts stop sperm from reaching the urethra.
wrong: The semen has no sperm because the testes are removed during a vasectomy.
The semen has no sperm because the sex glands stop making fluid after a vasectomy.

questions.q: Which is an effect on the baby of smoking during pregnancy?
questions.explain: Smoking during pregnancy reduces the oxygen reaching the foetus. The baby may grow less and have a low birth weight.
questions.lo: State the negative effects of substance abuse on the foetus

notes.0: Smoking harms the baby's development. It does not improve the growth of the lungs.
notes.1: Smoking slows the growth of the foetus. The baby is more likely to be smaller, not bigger.
notes.2: Smoking harms the developing baby. It does not make the baby's defences against disease stronger.

why.right: Smoking leads to low birth weight because less oxygen reaches the foetus, so it grows less.
wrong: Smoking leads to low birth weight because the smoke fills the uterus and squeezes the foetus.
Smoking leads to low birth weight because the foetus breathes in the smoke through its own lungs.

questions.q: A premature baby may need intensive care because
choices: its organs may not be fully developed
its immune system is too strong
it has too many red blood cells
questions.explain: A premature baby is born too early. Its organs, such as the lungs, may not be fully developed, so it may need help to survive.
questions.lo: State the negative effects of substance abuse on the foetus

notes.1: A premature baby's defences against disease are weaker than normal, not too strong.
notes.2: A premature baby is still growing. It needs care because its body is not yet fully ready.
notes.3: Being born early does not give a baby too many red blood cells. The concern is that the body is not fully ready.

why.right: A premature baby needs intensive care because it was born before its organs finished developing in the uterus.
wrong: A premature baby needs intensive care because it was born after its organs had stopped growing.
A premature baby needs intensive care because it was born with too much oxygen in its blood.

questions.q: A woman often drank alcohol during pregnancy. Her child may later
choices: find it hard to pay attention
questions.explain: Alcohol passes from the mother's blood to the foetus and can harm the developing brain. The child may later find it hard to pay attention.
questions.lo: State the negative effects of substance abuse on the foetus

notes.0: Alcohol harms the developing baby. It does not make the lungs stronger.
notes.2: Alcohol can slow the growth of the baby. It does not make a child grow taller.
notes.3: Alcohol harms the developing baby. It does not protect the child against infections.

why.right: The child may have attention problems because alcohol reached the foetus and harmed its developing brain.
wrong: The child may have attention problems because alcohol made the foetus grow too quickly in the uterus.
The child may have attention problems because alcohol stayed in the child's stomach after birth.

questions.q: An abortion is
choices: the deliberate ending of a pregnancy
questions.explain: An abortion is the deliberate ending of a pregnancy by removing the embryo or foetus from the uterus.
questions.lo: State the consequences of abortion and pre-marital sex

notes.0: Birth control methods prevent a pregnancy from starting. An abortion happens after a pregnancy has begun.
notes.1: Permanent birth control methods prevent any future pregnancy. An abortion happens after a pregnancy has begun.
notes.3: The release of an egg is ovulation. An abortion happens after a pregnancy has begun.

questions.q: Which is a possible consequence of an abortion?
questions.explain: An abortion can damage the uterus or cause an infection. This may make it difficult for the woman to have children later.
questions.lo: State the consequences of abortion and pre-marital sex

notes.0: An abortion does not make the ovaries release more eggs.
notes.1: An abortion does not protect against sexually transmitted infections.
notes.2: An abortion can damage the uterus. It does not make the uterus stronger.

why.right: Infertility may follow an abortion because the procedure can damage the uterus or cause an infection.
wrong: Infertility may follow an abortion because the procedure always removes both of the ovaries.
Infertility may follow an abortion because the procedure stops the body from making sex hormones.

questions.q: Which is a possible consequence of pre-marital sex?
questions.explain: Pre-marital sex can lead to an unwanted pregnancy. It can also spread sexually transmitted infections.
questions.lo: State the consequences of abortion and pre-marital sex

notes.1: Pre-marital sex increases the risk of infections that can cause infertility. It does not lower this risk.
notes.2: Sexual intercourse is the main way STIs spread. It does not protect against them.
notes.3: Sexual intercourse does not strengthen the immune system. It carries risks such as infections.

questions.q: What is the best way to avoid both unwanted pregnancy and STIs?
questions.explain: Abstinence means not having sexual intercourse. It is the only method that fully prevents both pregnancy and STIs.
questions.lo: State the consequences of abortion and pre-marital sex

notes.0: The rhythm method is not reliable and gives no protection against STIs.
notes.2: Birth control pills reduce the chance of pregnancy but give no protection against STIs.
notes.3: Spermicide kills sperm but gives no protection against STIs and is not fully reliable.

why.right: Abstinence works best because without sexual intercourse, sperm and STI germs cannot pass between partners.
wrong: Abstinence works best because it kills any sperm and germs that are already in the body.
Abstinence works best because it stops the ovaries from releasing any eggs.

questions.q: STIs are mainly transmitted through
questions.explain: STIs are sexually transmitted infections. They are mainly passed from one person to another through sexual intercourse.
questions.lo: State how STIs spread and the harmful consequences of syphilis, gonorrhoea and AIDS

notes.1: STI germs are passed in body fluids. They are not spread by shaking hands.
notes.2: STI germs are passed in body fluids. They are not spread by sharing objects such as textbooks.
notes.3: Coughing and sneezing spread infections such as influenza. STIs are passed on in a different way.

why.right: STIs spread through sexual intercourse because their germs pass between people in body fluids during sexual contact.
wrong: STIs spread through sexual intercourse because their germs float in the air around the reproductive organs.
STIs spread through sexual intercourse because their germs are made by the body during sexual contact.

questions.q: Which can spread HIV from one person to another?
questions.explain: HIV is carried in blood and some other body fluids. Sharing a needle used by an infected person can pass the virus on.
questions.lo: State how STIs spread and the harmful consequences of syphilis, gonorrhoea and AIDS

notes.0: HIV is not spread through hugging. The virus is passed on in blood and some other body fluids.
notes.2: HIV is not spread through shaking hands. The virus is passed on in blood and some other body fluids.
notes.3: HIV is not spread by sitting near someone. The virus is passed on in blood and some other body fluids.

why.right: Sharing a needle spreads HIV because the needle can carry infected blood into another person's body.
wrong: Sharing a needle spreads HIV because the needle itself produces the virus each time it is used.
Sharing a needle spreads HIV because the virus travels through the air around the used needle.

questions.q: Which is a long-term effect of syphilis?
questions.explain: Untreated syphilis can damage the brain and nerves over many years, leading to paralysis.
questions.lo: State how STIs spread and the harmful consequences of syphilis, gonorrhoea and AIDS

notes.0: A burning sensation when urinating is an early sign of gonorrhoea. It is not a long-term effect of syphilis.
notes.1: Flu-like symptoms appear early in some infections. A long-term effect develops much later and is more serious.
notes.2: A discharge of pus is an early sign of gonorrhoea. It is not a long-term effect of syphilis.

questions.q: Which is a long-term effect of gonorrhoea?
questions.explain: Untreated gonorrhoea can damage the reproductive organs and lead to infertility.
questions.lo: State how STIs spread and the harmful consequences of syphilis, gonorrhoea and AIDS

notes.0: AIDS is caused by HIV, a virus. Gonorrhoea is caused by bacteria and does not lead to AIDS.
notes.1: Blindness from gonorrhoea is mainly a risk for babies born to infected mothers. The long-term effect on the infected adult is on the reproductive organs.
notes.3: Paralysis is a long-term effect of untreated syphilis. Gonorrhoea affects a different part of the body.

questions.q: If left untreated, HIV can develop into
questions.explain: HIV is the virus that causes AIDS. If left untreated, HIV infection develops into AIDS.
questions.lo: State how STIs spread and the harmful consequences of syphilis, gonorrhoea and AIDS

notes.1: Syphilis is a separate infection caused by bacteria. HIV does not turn into it.
notes.2: Influenza is caused by a different virus that spreads through the air. HIV does not turn into it.
notes.3: Gonorrhoea is a separate infection caused by bacteria. HIV does not turn into it.

questions.q: A person has a burning sensation when urinating and pus discharge. Which STI is likely?
questions.explain: A burning sensation when urinating and a discharge of pus are common signs of gonorrhoea.
questions.lo: State how STIs spread and the harmful consequences of syphilis, gonorrhoea and AIDS

notes.0: Syphilis usually begins with a painless sore. A burning sensation and pus are signs of a different STI.
notes.1: HIV infection often causes flu-like symptoms at first. A burning sensation and pus are signs of a different STI.

questions.q: Which birth control method also reduces the spread of STIs?
questions.explain: A condom forms a barrier, so sperm and body fluids do not pass between partners. This reduces the spread of STIs.
questions.lo: State how STIs spread and the harmful consequences of syphilis, gonorrhoea and AIDS

notes.0: A diaphragm covers the cervix but does not stop contact with body fluids. It does not protect against STIs.
notes.1: An intra-uterine device works inside the uterus. It does not stop contact with body fluids, so it does not protect against STIs.
notes.2: Birth control pills act on the release of eggs. They do not stop contact with body fluids, so they do not protect against STIs.

why.right: A condom reduces the spread of STIs because it is a barrier that stops body fluids passing between partners.
wrong: A condom reduces the spread of STIs because it contains antibiotics that kill all the germs.
A condom reduces the spread of STIs because it stops the ovaries from releasing eggs.

questions.q: Antibiotics can
choices: kill bacteria or stop their growth
questions.explain: Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them from growing. They do not work on viruses.
questions.lo: State that bacterial STIs can be cured by antibiotics but viral STIs cannot

notes.0: Killing sperm is what spermicide does. Antibiotics are medicines used against one type of germ.
notes.2: Preventing ovulation is what birth control pills do. Antibiotics are medicines used against one type of germ.
notes.3: Antibiotics do not work against viruses. They act on a different type of germ.

questions.q: Which infection can be treated with antibiotics?
questions.explain: Gonorrhoea is caused by bacteria, so it can be treated with antibiotics.
questions.lo: State that bacterial STIs can be cured by antibiotics but viral STIs cannot

notes.0: Influenza is caused by a virus. Antibiotics do not work on viruses.
notes.2: HIV is a virus. Antibiotics do not work on viruses.

why.right: Gonorrhoea can be treated with antibiotics because it is caused by bacteria, which antibiotics can kill.
wrong: Gonorrhoea can be treated with antibiotics because it is caused by a virus, which antibiotics can kill.
Gonorrhoea can be treated with antibiotics because antibiotics can cure every type of infection.

questions.q: Which STI cannot be cured with antibiotics?
questions.explain: HIV is a virus. Antibiotics kill bacteria and do not work on viruses, so they cannot cure HIV.
questions.lo: State that bacterial STIs can be cured by antibiotics but viral STIs cannot

notes.0: Gonorrhoea is caused by bacteria, so antibiotics can cure it. Think about which STI is caused by a virus.
notes.1: Syphilis is caused by bacteria, so antibiotics can cure it. Think about which STI is caused by a virus.

why.right: HIV cannot be cured with antibiotics because it is a virus, and antibiotics work only on bacteria.
wrong: HIV cannot be cured with antibiotics because it is a bacterium that has grown too large to kill.
HIV cannot be cured with antibiotics because it hides in the reproductive organs where medicine cannot reach.

questions.q: A patient with HIV is given antibiotics. Will this cure the infection?
choices: no, because HIV is a virus
yes, because HIV is a virus
no, because HIV is a bacterium
yes, because HIV is a bacterium
questions.explain: HIV is a virus. Antibiotics act only on bacteria, so they will not cure HIV.
questions.lo: State that bacterial STIs can be cured by antibiotics but viral STIs cannot

notes.1: Antibiotics do not work on viruses. Being a virus is a reason for antibiotics to fail, not to succeed.
notes.2: HIV is not a bacterium. Check what type of germ HIV is.
notes.3: HIV is not a bacterium. Check what type of germ HIV is and whether antibiotics act on that type.

why.right: Antibiotics will not cure HIV because they act on bacteria, and HIV is a virus.
wrong: Antibiotics will not cure HIV because they act on viruses, and HIV is a bacterium.
Antibiotics will not cure HIV because they act only on infections of the lungs.

questions.q: Which is a reason for the growing world population?
questions.explain: Advances in medicine, such as vaccines and antibiotics, help people survive diseases and live longer. This makes the world population grow.
questions.lo: Suggest reasons for the growing world population

notes.0: Poorer sanitation spreads disease and causes more deaths. That would slow population growth, not speed it up.
notes.1: Less food would lead to hunger and more deaths. That would slow population growth, not speed it up.
notes.2: More disease outbreaks cause more deaths. That would slow population growth, not speed it up.

why.right: Advances in medicine increase the population because fewer people die from disease and people live longer.
wrong: Advances in medicine increase the population because medicines make each woman release more eggs.
Advances in medicine increase the population because medicines make people need less food to survive.

questions.q: Ships brought food and medicines to more places. Which reason is this?
questions.explain: Ships carrying food and medicines to more places is an example of improved transportation.
questions.lo: Suggest reasons for the growing world population

notes.0: Increased food production means growing more food. The ships moved food but did not grow it.
notes.1: Medical advancements are new discoveries in medicine. The ships moved medicines but did not discover them.
notes.3: Improved sanitation is about clean water and the safe removal of waste. The ships moved goods.

why.right: This is improved transportation because ships moved food and medicines to people who could not get them before.
wrong: This is improved transportation because ships discovered new medicines on their long journeys.
This is improved transportation because ships cleaned the water supply in the places they reached.

questions.q: Flush toilets reduced the spread of cholera and typhoid. Which reason is this?
questions.explain: Flush toilets remove human waste safely. This is improved sanitation, which reduces the spread of diseases such as cholera and typhoid.
questions.lo: Suggest reasons for the growing world population

notes.0: Medical advancements are new medicines and treatments. Flush toilets prevent disease in a different way.
notes.1: Increased food production means growing more food. Flush toilets are not about food supply.
notes.2: Improved transportation is about moving people and goods. Flush toilets are not about transport.

why.right: This is improved sanitation because flush toilets remove human waste that spreads diseases such as cholera.
wrong: This is improved sanitation because flush toilets contain medicines that cure diseases such as cholera.
This is improved sanitation because flush toilets carry food and clean water to more homes.

questions.q: Vaccines protected people against smallpox. Which reason is this?
questions.explain: Vaccines are a medical advancement. They protect people against diseases such as smallpox, so fewer people die.
questions.lo: Suggest reasons for the growing world population

notes.0: Improved transportation is about moving people and goods. Vaccines are not about transport.
notes.2: Improved sanitation is about clean water and the safe removal of waste. Vaccines protect people in a different way.
notes.3: Increased food production means growing more food. Vaccines are not about food supply.

why.right: This is a medical advancement because vaccines are a medical discovery that protects people from disease.
wrong: This is a medical advancement because vaccines remove the waste that spreads smallpox.
This is a medical advancement because vaccines carry food to places where smallpox is found.
